newsitem.title: GERMANY: German extremists on left and right use Internet.
newsitem.headline: German extremists on left and right use Internet.

text.p: Extremist groups on both the left and the right are making increased use of the uncensored Internet to distribute propaganda and communicate among themselves, Germany's anti-extremist watchdog said on Tuesday.

The international computer network not only permits efficient communication to take place outside the authorities' reach, but also allows the distribution of racist and subversive texts which it would be almost impossible to publish in Germany.

"The Internet is likely to gain substantial importance in coming years for the distribution of extreme right-wing propaganda and for the co-ordination of activities in the extreme right-wing scene," the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution said in its 1996 annual report.

Left-wing groups had found the net "ideal for co-ordinating international protests" and even used it to distribute instructions for sabotaging trains -- a favourite recent tactic on anti-nuclear protesters.
German authorities have found it practically impossible to apply domestic legal restrictions to Internet publications fed into the network from abroad.

The most glaring example is Toronto-based German neo-Nazi Ernst Zuendel, who has used his Internet homepage, featuring audio and video sequences, to publish texts denying the mass execution of Jews in the Holocaust.
Germany has placed the page on its index of publications restricted for juveniles, but this amounts to little more than an appeal not to let young people read it.
Authorities have had some success in limiting the use of electronic mailboxes for extremist communications, but are now being outfoxed by coded messages, the report said.

Left-wing groups have used the Internet to co-ordinate militant opposition to nuclear waste dumping -- leading to spectacular campaigns which have forced authorities to deploy tens of thousands of police to ensure safe passage of trains carrying nuclear waste.
The anti-nuclear campaign led to a 14 percent rise in violent crimes attributed to left-wing extremists last year, to 654.

The number of right-wing and racist crimes rose 11 percent to 8,730, largely because members of the public are increasingly prepared to report the distribution of right-wing propaganda, the report said.
But instances of right-wing violence fell for the fourth year running, to 781 from 837 in 1995 and a peak of 2,639 in 1992, following German unification.
Since then the government has waged a successful police and publicity offensive to stem the rise in racism.
The number of recorded anti-foreigner attacks fell 18 percent in 1996 to 441.
There were 29 recorded instances of anti-Semitic violence and 817 other anti-Semitic crimes, compared to 27 and 1,128 respectively last year.
However, while the number of right-wing extremists and neo-Nazis fell by two percent to 45,300, the number prepared to engage in violence rose by about 200 to 6,400, the report said.
